summary: A 1969 outline for the software that would sit between a host computer and its IMP. It splits the job into a network program and a handler program, and lists questions for discussion. The original was handwritten and later retyped as a reconstruction, so it is a historical design sketch.

eli5.summary: This note plans the small helper program that lets a big computer talk to the box that connects it to the network, like planning a mailroom.

questions: what is the host imp interface
what is a host heading in the arpanet
how big was an early arpanet message
subtitle: A 1969 sketch of the two programs that move a host computer's messages to and from its IMP.

tldr.problem: A host computer needs software to turn its users' send requests into messages the IMP, the network's message-handling machine, will accept, and to drive the channel hardware that connects the two.
tldr.mechanism: Split the job into a Network program that multiplexes user requests, builds a 16-bit host heading and fills buffers, and a short Handler program that drives the channel hardware. They share a pool of buffers and an interface table.
tldr.outcome: This is a preliminary design outline written for discussion, and it ends with open questions rather than answers. The original was handwritten and the text on the site is a reconstruction.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 7 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a historical design sketch from May 1969, and the site text is a reconstruction of a handwritten original.

sections.title: Two Programs and Shared Tables
sections.content:
RFC 7 outlines the software design for the Host-IMP interface, based on a study of BBN Report No. 763. The system rests on two main programs: the Handler program, which drives the channel hardware unit, and the Network program, which carries out the user's transmission requests.

Because communication is full duplex, each program has an output part and an input part. The two programs exchange data through a pool of buffers and logical information through an interface table. The RFC only works out the output side and says the input side would be very similar.
sections.eli5: Two helpers share a table and a pile of boxes. One packs what people want to send. The other carries the boxes to the network.

sections.title: What the Network Program Does to Outgoing Text
sections.content:
The Network program multiplexes outgoing messages and distributes incoming ones, using link identification numbers (a link is a logical connection between two users). A user's program supplies the text location, the text length in bytes and the destination.

The Network program then prepares a 16-bit host heading: 1 trace bit, 2 spare bits, an 8-bit link number and a 5-bit destination host. It inserts a 16-bit marking, a one preceded by fifteen zeros, so the text starts on a word boundary. If the text exceeds 1006 bytes (8080 bits less 32 bits of heading and marking, divided by 8) it is broken into several messages, each with its own heading. It also transcodes EBCDIC characters to ASCII, fills the buffers and updates the interface table.
sections.eli5: Before mailing, the helper writes an address label, adds a little padding so the letter starts neatly, and cuts a long letter into several envelopes if it is too big.

sections.title: Handler, Buffers and Interface Table
sections.content:
The Handler program is started by the Network program or by an I/O interrupt. It is expected to be very short, coded in master mode (privileged instructions) and integrated in the I/O supervisor of the operating system. It controls the channel hardware, empties the buffers the Network program has filled, and reads and updates the interface table.

Each buffer must hold the largest host message text plus heading and marking (1006 + 4 = 1010 bytes), so the RFC suggests 256 words (1024 bytes). The interface table could be a ring with two pointers, one for filling (moved by the Network program) and one for extracting (moved by the Handler). Each entry holds a buffer address and a byte count.
sections.eli5: The carrier only follows the table: it picks up the next box, takes it to the mailbox, and crosses it off the list.

sections.title: Open Questions
sections.content:
The outline closes with questions. Why is there no simple control procedure between the host and the IMP, and what happens if a message reaches the IMP with a transmission error? From the BBN specifications the error appears to be passed on to the receiving host, so the author asks whether a host-to-host control procedure is needed.

It also asks where the special channel hardware unit will be attached and how the Handler learns the length of an incoming message. A last question asks when documentation will be available to design the interface between user programs and the Network program.
sections.eli5: The author ends by asking the group what to do when a letter gets smudged on the way, and where the mailbox should be bolted on.
